points: The viviparous lizard is a Eurasian lizard.
The viviparous lizard is also called the common lizard.
Its scientific name is Zootoca vivipara.
It lives farther north than any other reptile species that is neither marine nor avian.
The species can give birth to live young.
The species can also reproduce by laying eggs.
The species gets its common name from its ability to give birth to live young.
Zootoca means 'live birth' in Latinized Greek.
Vivipara means 'live birth' in Latin.
The species was formerly called Lacerta vivipara.
The genus Lacerta was split in 2007.
The split of Lacerta produced nine genera.
Arnold, Arribas, and Carranza carried out the split of Lacerta.
The viviparous lizard actively regulates its body temperature even in very cold climates instead of simply letting it track the surroundings.
The viviparous lizard has the largest geographic range of any lizard species.
Its range includes subarctic regions.
Individuals can survive freezing in especially cold conditions.
Frozen individuals often thaw about two months later.
The lizards use sites where local geological conditions keep their surroundings warmer.
The viviparous lizard is small.
Its average length ranges from 50 to 77 mm (2 to 3 inches).
Its average mass ranges from 2 to 5 g (0.1 to 0.2 ounces).
The species has no single characteristic color.
Individuals can be brown.
Individuals can be red.
Individuals can be gray.
Individuals can be green.
Individuals can be black.
Males and females differ in several physical traits.
Distinct color forms occur more commonly in females than in males.
Females have three underside color forms within a population.
One female color form has a pale yellow underside.
One female color form has a bright orange underside.
One female color form has a mixture of yellow and orange on the underside.
Researchers have proposed several explanations for why the color forms exist.
One proposed explanation links the color forms to temperature regulation.
One proposed explanation links the color forms to avoiding predators.
One proposed explanation links the color forms to social cues related to reproduction.
An experiment by Vercken and colleagues supported the social-cue explanation over temperature regulation and predator avoidance.
Female underside color is associated with patterns of sexual reproduction.
Female underside color is associated with how offspring are distributed between the sexes.
The male underside is typically brighter and more colorful than the female underside.
The male underside can show yellow.
The male underside can show orange.
The male underside can show green.
The male underside can show blue.
Males typically have spots along their backs.
Females typically have dark stripes along their backs.
Females typically have dark stripes along their sides.
Males have larger heads than females.
The evidence suggests that head size in males is subject to sexual selection.
Males with larger heads are more successful at mating than males with smaller heads.
Males with larger heads are more successful in encounters with other males.
Larger males reproduce more often within a mating season than smaller males do.
The lizards flick their tongues in the presence of a predator.
Females behave aggressively toward one another.
Aggression between females appears to depend on the color of their side stripes.
The species is terrestrial and spends most of its time on the ground.
The lizards occasionally visit higher sites.
The lizards spend much of their time basking in the sun to regulate their body temperature.
The lizards hibernate in cold weather to maintain suitable body temperatures.
Their hibernation period runs from October to March.
Heathland is a typical habitat.
Moorland is a typical habitat.
Woodland is a typical habitat.
Grassland is a typical habitat.
The species is native to much of northern Eurasia.
In Europe, the species occurs mainly north of the Alps and the Carpathians.
Its range includes the British Isles.
Its range excludes Iceland.
Its range includes parts of northern Iberia.
Its range includes parts of the Balkans.
In Asia, its range lies mostly in Russia.
Its range excludes northern Siberia.
Its range includes northern Kazakhstan.
Its range includes Mongolia.
Its range includes China.
Its range includes Japan.
It is Ireland's only native terrestrial reptile.
Individual home ranges extend from 539 to 1,692 square meters.
Males generally have larger home ranges than females.
Home-range size depends on population density.
Home-range size depends on the presence of prey.
The article describes the species as exclusively insectivorous, unlike many other lizards.
The lizards eat flies.
The lizards eat spiders.
The lizards eat insects in the order Hemiptera.
Cicadas are one example of the hemipterans they eat.
The lizards eat moth larvae.
The lizards eat mealworms.
The lizards actively hunt all of their prey.
One study found that females ate more than males after accounting for body size.
Feeding rates rose with increasing sunshine.
Birds are common predators of the species.
Great grey shrikes (Lanius excubitor) preferentially preyed on adult males over adult females.
Great grey shrikes preferentially preyed on adult males over juveniles.
Greater activity by adult males during the breeding season may explain why great grey shrikes take more of them.
Birds of prey hunt the lizards.
Crows hunt the lizards.
Snakes hunt the lizards.
Shrikes are among the lizard's predators.
Hedgehogs hunt the lizards.
Shrews hunt the lizards.
Foxes hunt the lizards.
Domestic cats hunt the lizards.
The lizards can be infested by helminths.
Helminths are parasitic worms.
The diversity of parasite species in a lizard depends on its diet.
A study found that individuals with more carnivorous diets had less diverse parasite populations.
Larger lizards carried more parasites in the study.
The viviparous lizard can be infected by blood parasites.
One study found blood parasites in 39.8% of the viviparous lizards sampled.
The same study found blood parasites in 22.3% of the Lacerta agilis individuals sampled.
The study found no significant difference in blood parasite infection between male and female viviparous lizards.
Scientists disagree about how live birth evolved in the viviparous lizard.
Some scientists argue that live birth evolved from egg-laying only once.
Proponents of a single origin consider a return to egg-laying possible but rare.
Research by Yann Surget-Groba suggests that live birth evolved independently from egg-laying in multiple lineages of the species.
Surget-Groba's research suggests that the species reverted to egg-laying two or three times.
Surget-Groba argues that reversions to egg-laying are less rare than previously believed.
Live-bearing populations extend from France to Russia.
The article identifies northern Spain and southwestern France as the only places with egg-laying populations.
Some research in the Italian Alps suggests that distinct egg-laying and live-bearing populations should be classified as separate species.
Cornetti and colleagues reported their findings in 2015.
Cornetti and colleagues found that live-bearing and egg-laying populations in contact in the Italian Alps were reproductively isolated.
Laboratory crosses between live-bearing and egg-laying individuals produced embryonic malformations.
The laboratory crosses nevertheless produced hybrid offspring.
Hybrid females retained embryos in the uterus much longer than egg-laying females did.
The embryos retained by hybrid females were surrounded by thin shells.
The shells around those embryos were translucent.
The lizards reach sexual maturity in their second year.
Males are infertile for the first two weeks after hibernation ends.
Larger males produce more sperm during the breeding season than smaller males do.
Larger males have fewer sperm left at the end of the breeding season than smaller males do.
At higher altitudes, exclusively egg-laying populations generally start breeding later.
At higher altitudes, exclusively egg-laying populations generally lay fewer clutches per breeding season.
High-altitude egg-laying females often lay just one clutch per breeding season.
The species typically lives for five to six years.
The males measured in one study had an average head width of 5.6 mm (0.22 inches).
The males measured in that study had an average head length of 10.5 mm (0.41 inches).
The females measured in that study had an average head width of 5.3 mm (0.21 inches).
The females measured in that study had an average head length of 9.7 mm (0.38 inches).
The first stage of courtship is called 'Capture.'
During Capture, the male grips the female with his mouth and jaws to begin mating.
Greater head length is associated with greater mating success in males.
Greater head width is associated with greater mating success in males.
Males use their heads as weapons in fights with other males.
Larger heads are typically more effective in fights between males.
Aggression between males centers on access to mates.
Males with smaller heads have significantly less access to females for mating.
Active thermoregulation helps the lizards keep their body temperatures within a suitable range in subarctic habitats.
Species often adopt thermoconformity in extreme temperatures.
Thermoconformity means surviving ambient temperatures without actively regulating body temperature.
In extreme environments, the costs of actively regulating body temperature can outweigh the benefits.
Thermoregulation helps the viviparous lizard move effectively.
Thermoregulation helps the viviparous lizard escape danger.
Thermoregulation supports other behaviors needed for survival.
The lizard's ways of coping with cold help it continue to thermoregulate in harsh environments.
Local geological warming helps the species survive in habitats that would otherwise be too cold.
The lizards can spend the winter in a supercooled state without freezing.
Supercooled individuals froze completely when temperatures dropped below −3 °C (27 °F).
Frozen individuals thaw when warmer weather returns.
Unfrozen groundwater warms and moderates the temperature of the soil even when the subarctic air is very cold.
The lizards find warmer microhabitats that stay above the freezing point of their body fluids.
The lizards can hibernate in the upper layers of the soil.
The lizards can hibernate at temperatures as low as −10 °C (14 °F).
Cold hardiness helps explain the species' wide distribution across the Palearctic.
Groundwater-warmed soil helps explain the species' wide distribution across the Palearctic.
Female color forms have received relatively little study despite extensive research on the species.
Female color forms are inherited from the mother.
An individual retains the same color form throughout its life.
Genotype helps determine an individual's color form.
Environmental conditions help determine an individual's color form.
Population density affects how prevalent the different color forms are.
The relative frequencies of the color forms influence how common those forms are in the population.
Population density affects reproductive fitness.
The relative frequencies of the color forms affect reproductive fitness.
Clutch size is one measure of reproductive fitness discussed in the article.
Offspring sex ratio is one measure of reproductive fitness discussed in the article.
Hatching success is one measure of reproductive fitness discussed in the article.
Multiple color forms are more prevalent in lower-density populations.
The article attributes the prevalence of multiple color forms at low density to the lizards doing well when competition within the species is low.
Greater competition between individuals lowers survival rates.
Females disperse through habitats depending on how common the existing color forms are.
Yellow females produce fewer offspring than either orange or mixed-color females.
Orange females produce fewer offspring than mixed-color females.
Orange females are particularly sensitive to competition with other members of the species.
Orange females are particularly sensitive to competition that depends on the color forms present.
Orange females lay smaller clutches when overall population density is high.
Orange females usually lay smaller clutches when yellow females are more numerous.
Smaller clutches may allow orange females to conserve energy for survival.
Smaller clutches may allow orange females to conserve energy for reproduction.
A trade-off between clutch size and offspring size helps the orange form persist.
Offspring from smaller clutches are often larger.
Larger offspring are more likely to survive.
Larger individuals have an advantage in physical competition.
Natural selection can favor larger individuals because of their competitive advantage.
Yellow females produce large clutches early in life.
Hatching success declines as yellow females age.
Declining reproductive viability leaves yellow females with fewer offspring over their lifetimes.
Large clutches help the yellow form persist by increasing its frequency in the population.
Selection favors the yellow form because large clutches improve its fitness.
Reproductive success in mixed-color females is less sensitive to competition.
Reproductive success in mixed-color females is less sensitive to the relative frequencies of the color forms.
Mixed-color females combine the large-clutch advantage of yellow females with the large-size and competitive advantages of orange females.
Mixed-color females can maintain high reproductive success while producing large clutches.
Mixed-color females can maintain high hatching success while producing large clutches.
Selection helps the mixed-color form persist because of its high fitness.
Each of the three female color forms has evolutionary advantages.

question.text: A researcher observes one population laying eggs and another giving birth to live young. How does the article explain these observations?
options: Only the live-bearing population can be a population of the viviparous lizard.
Both observations fit the article's account of the viviparous lizard, which includes both egg-laying and live-bearing populations.
Only the egg-laying population can be a population of the viviparous lizard.
Both observations fit only if every female lays eggs before giving birth to live young in the same breeding season.
